name.text: What the Definition of Ready is

questiontext.text: What is the Definition of Ready (DoR)?

answer.text: The shared criteria a backlog item must meet before the team pulls it into a sprint

feedback.text: Correct — the DoR is the entry gate: it says when an item is ready to be started.

answer.text: The shared criteria for deciding when a piece of work is truly complete

feedback.text: That describes the Definition of Done, the exit gate, not the DoR.

answer.text: The specific behaviours a single story must exhibit to be accepted

feedback.text: Those are that story's acceptance criteria, not the DoR itself.

answer.text: The order in which items appear in the product backlog

feedback.text: Backlog ordering is prioritisation, not the readiness gate.

generalfeedback.text: The Definition of Ready is a shared, agreed checklist a backlog item must satisfy before the team commits to it in a sprint — for example it is clear, has testable acceptance criteria, is estimated, is small enough to finish in a sprint, and its dependencies are resolved. It is the entry gate that keeps vague, unready work out of the sprint.

name.text: What the Definition of Done is

questiontext.text: What is the Definition of Done (DoD)?

answer.text: The shared criteria for when a piece of work is truly complete

feedback.text: Correct — the DoD is the exit gate that defines what "complete" really means.

answer.text: The shared criteria a story must meet before it is pulled into a sprint

feedback.text: That is the Definition of Ready, the entry gate, not the DoD.

answer.text: The list of specific behaviours a single story must satisfy

feedback.text: Those are that story's acceptance criteria; the DoD is a generic quality bar.

answer.text: The estimate, in story points, of how large a story is

feedback.text: Sizing is part of readiness, not the definition of completeness.

generalfeedback.text: The Definition of Done is a shared, agreed set of criteria that must all hold before work counts as complete — for example code written and reviewed, unit and acceptance tests passing, work integrated, docs updated, and no known critical defects. It is the exit gate that stops unfinished work being called "Done".

name.text: DoR is which kind of gate

questiontext.text: The Definition of Ready acts as which kind of gate?

answer.text: An entry gate, controlling whether work is ready to be started

feedback.text: Correct — DoR governs entry: it decides when an item may be pulled into a sprint.

answer.text: An exit gate, controlling whether work is complete

feedback.text: The exit gate is the Definition of Done, not the DoR.

answer.text: A gate that applies only after the work has been released

feedback.text: DoR applies before work starts, not after release.

answer.text: A gate owned solely by the product owner and hidden from the team

feedback.text: The DoR is shared and team-owned, not a hidden personal checklist.

generalfeedback.text: DoR is the entry gate. It is applied when the team is about to pull an item into a sprint, ensuring the item is understood, sized, and ready. This prevents starting vague or unready work.

name.text: DoD is which kind of gate

questiontext.text: The Definition of Done acts as which kind of gate?

answer.text: An exit gate, controlling whether work may be called complete

feedback.text: Correct — DoD governs exit: it decides when work is truly Done.

answer.text: An entry gate, controlling whether work is ready to start

feedback.text: The entry gate is the Definition of Ready, not the DoD.

answer.text: A gate that only limits how many items are in the backlog

feedback.text: The DoD concerns completeness of work, not backlog size.

answer.text: A gate that measures how fast the team writes code

feedback.text: The DoD is a quality bar for completeness, not a speed metric.

generalfeedback.text: DoD is the exit gate. It is applied when the team wants to declare work complete, ensuring the agreed quality criteria are met. This prevents calling unfinished work "Done".

name.text: DoR is checked before pulling a story in

questiontext.text: The Definition of Ready is checked before a story is pulled into a sprint.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — DoR is the entry gate, applied before committing to the work.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: DoR is precisely the check made before the team pulls an item into a sprint.

generalfeedback.text: The DoR is the entry gate. The team checks it during backlog refinement and sprint planning, before committing to an item, so that only ready work enters the sprint.

name.text: DoD decides whether work is complete

questiontext.text: The Definition of Done is used to decide whether a piece of work may be considered complete.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — DoD is the exit gate that defines completeness.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Deciding completeness is exactly what the DoD is for.

generalfeedback.text: The DoD is the exit gate. Work counts as complete only when every DoD criterion holds, keeping the meaning of "Done" honest and consistent.

name.text: What acceptance criteria are

questiontext.text: What are a story's acceptance criteria?

answer.text: The specific, testable conditions describing what that particular story must do

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance criteria are per-story and specific to that story's behaviour.

answer.text: The generic quality bar that every story in the team must meet

feedback.text: That is the Definition of Done; acceptance criteria are specific to one story.

answer.text: The rule for how many stories may be in progress at once

feedback.text: That is a work-in-progress limit, not acceptance criteria.

answer.text: The estimate of how many hours the story will take

feedback.text: That is an estimate; acceptance criteria describe required behaviour, not effort.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance criteria are the specific, testable conditions that define what a single story must do to be accepted. They are per-story and vary from story to story, unlike the DoD, which is a generic bar applied to every story.

name.text: Which gate applies when starting a story

questiontext.text: When the team is deciding whether it may start a story, which gate applies?

answer.text: The Definition of Ready

feedback.text: Correct — readiness to start is governed by the DoR entry gate.

answer.text: The Definition of Done

feedback.text: The DoD applies when finishing, not when starting.

answer.text: Neither — starting a story needs no gate

feedback.text: Starting is exactly where the DoR entry gate applies.

answer.text: Both apply equally at the moment of starting

feedback.text: Only the DoR applies at the start; the DoD is for completion.

generalfeedback.text: Starting a story is an entry decision, so the Definition of Ready applies. The Definition of Done is the exit gate and is only relevant when deciding whether the story is complete.

name.text: Which gate applies when completing a story

questiontext.text: When the team is deciding whether a story may be called complete, which gate applies?

answer.text: The Definition of Done

feedback.text: Correct — completion is governed by the DoD exit gate.

answer.text: The Definition of Ready

feedback.text: The DoR applies when starting, not when finishing.

answer.text: Neither — completeness is a matter of personal opinion

feedback.text: Completeness is judged against the DoD, not personal opinion.

answer.text: Whichever gate the developer prefers at the time

feedback.text: The gate is fixed: completion is judged by the DoD.

generalfeedback.text: Deciding completeness is an exit decision, so the Definition of Done applies. The DoR governed whether the work should have started; the DoD governs whether it is finished.

name.text: Is being estimated a DoR or DoD item

questiontext.text: "The story has been estimated and sized." Is this a Definition of Ready item or a Definition of Done item?

answer.text: A Definition of Ready item

feedback.text: Correct — being estimated is part of readiness to start, checked before the sprint.

answer.text: A Definition of Done item

feedback.text: Estimation happens before work starts; it is not a completeness criterion.

answer.text: Neither — it belongs to release notes

feedback.text: Sizing is a readiness concern, not release documentation.

answer.text: Both equally, at start and at completion

feedback.text: Estimation is a readiness (entry) concern, not a completion (exit) one.

generalfeedback.text: Being estimated and small enough to finish in a sprint are readiness concerns: they must hold before the team pulls the item in. They belong to the DoR entry gate, not the DoD.

name.text: Is code review a DoR or DoD item

questiontext.text: "The code has been reviewed." Is this a Definition of Ready item or a Definition of Done item?

answer.text: A Definition of Done item

feedback.text: Correct — code review is part of completing the work, an exit-gate criterion.

answer.text: A Definition of Ready item

feedback.text: There is no code to review before the story starts; review is a completion concern.

answer.text: Neither — it is only an estimate

feedback.text: Code review is a completeness criterion, not an estimate.

answer.text: An acceptance criterion specific to that one story

feedback.text: Review applies to every story generically, so it is a DoD item, not a per-story AC.

generalfeedback.text: Code review can only happen after code exists, so it is part of completing the work. It belongs to the DoD exit gate, and because it applies to every story it is a generic DoD item rather than a per-story acceptance criterion.

name.text: Done needs both acceptance criteria and DoD

questiontext.text: A story is only "Done" when it meets both its own acceptance criteria and the team's Definition of Done.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — Done requires satisfying the per-story acceptance criteria and the generic DoD.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Meeting only one of the two is not enough; Done needs both the AC and the DoD.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance criteria say what this specific story must do; the DoD is the generic quality bar for every story. A story is Done only when both hold: it does what was asked and it meets the shared quality standard.

name.text: Is testable acceptance criteria a DoR item

questiontext.text: "The story has clear, testable acceptance criteria defined." Before the sprint, which gate does this satisfy?

answer.text: The Definition of Ready — having testable acceptance criteria is part of readiness

feedback.text: Correct — a ready story must already have clear, testable acceptance criteria.

answer.text: The Definition of Done — it means the tests already pass

feedback.text: Having criteria defined is not the same as the tests passing; that comes at completion.

answer.text: Neither — acceptance criteria are irrelevant to readiness

feedback.text: Testable acceptance criteria are a core readiness requirement.

answer.text: It is a release-notes requirement

feedback.text: Defining acceptance criteria is a readiness concern, not release documentation.

generalfeedback.text: A ready story must have clear, testable acceptance criteria before it is pulled in — that is a DoR item. Note the distinction: having acceptance criteria defined is readiness (DoR), whereas the criteria actually being met is part of completion (DoD).

name.text: Are passing tests a DoD item

questiontext.text: "Unit and acceptance tests are written and passing." Which gate does this belong to?

answer.text: The Definition of Done

feedback.text: Correct — passing tests are part of completing the work, an exit-gate criterion.

answer.text: The Definition of Ready

feedback.text: Tests cannot pass before the work is built; this is a completion concern.

answer.text: Neither — it is just an estimate of effort

feedback.text: Passing tests are a completeness criterion, not an estimate.

answer.text: It is a readiness item because tests are mentioned

feedback.text: Mentioning tests does not make it readiness; passing tests is a completion criterion.

generalfeedback.text: Tests can only pass after the work is built, so "tests written and passing" is part of the DoD exit gate. Readiness only requires that testable acceptance criteria exist, not that tests already pass.

name.text: DoR and DoD are team-owned and evolve

questiontext.text: Both the Definition of Ready and the Definition of Done are meant to be team-owned, explicit, and allowed to evolve over time.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — both are shared, explicit team agreements that the team refines as it learns.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Both gates are team-owned, explicit, and expected to evolve; they are not fixed external rules.

generalfeedback.text: DoR and DoD are shared agreements the team makes explicit and revisits, typically in retrospectives. Keeping them owned by the team and evolving keeps them realistic and enforced rather than ignored.

name.text: Classify estimated with dependencies resolved

questiontext.text: A team's checklist says: "the story is estimated and its dependencies are resolved." Where does this criterion belong?

answer.text: The Definition of Ready — both are entry conditions checked before starting

feedback.text: Correct — estimation and resolved dependencies are readiness conditions.

answer.text: The Definition of Done — they describe completed work

feedback.text: Neither is about completeness; both must hold before the work begins.

answer.text: They are acceptance criteria for that one story

feedback.text: These are generic readiness conditions, not the story's specific behaviour.

answer.text: They belong only at the release gate

feedback.text: Estimation and dependency resolution gate entry to the sprint, not release.

generalfeedback.text: Being estimated and having dependencies identified and resolved are classic readiness conditions: they must be true before the team commits, so they belong to the DoR entry gate.

name.text: Classify reviewed and tests passing

questiontext.text: A checklist says: "the code is reviewed and its tests are passing." Where does this belong?

answer.text: The Definition of Done — both are completion conditions checked at the exit gate

feedback.text: Correct — review and passing tests are part of finishing the work.

answer.text: The Definition of Ready — both make the story ready to start

feedback.text: Neither can occur before the work is built; they are completion, not readiness.

answer.text: They are readiness conditions because they mention tests

feedback.text: Mentioning tests does not make it readiness; passing them is a completion concern.

answer.text: They only matter after the product is retired

feedback.text: They gate completion of the story, not product retirement.

generalfeedback.text: Code review and passing tests both require the work to already exist, so they are completion conditions belonging to the DoD exit gate — not readiness conditions.

name.text: Acceptance criteria versus DoD scope

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly contrasts acceptance criteria with the Definition of Done?

answer.text: Acceptance criteria are specific to one story; the DoD is generic and applies to every story

feedback.text: Correct — AC are per-story and specific; the DoD is a shared bar for all stories.

answer.text: The DoD is specific to one story; acceptance criteria apply to every story

feedback.text: This is reversed: AC are per-story, the DoD is generic.

answer.text: They are the same thing under two different names

feedback.text: They are distinct: AC describe this story, the DoD is the shared quality bar.

answer.text: Both are unique to each story and never shared

feedback.text: The DoD is shared across all stories, unlike per-story acceptance criteria.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance criteria describe what one particular story must do and differ from story to story. The DoD is a single generic quality bar applied to every story alike. This is why a story must meet both to be Done.

name.text: Why Done needs both AC and DoD

questiontext.text: Why must a story satisfy both its acceptance criteria and the DoD to be Done?

answer.text: Acceptance criteria prove it does the right thing; the DoD proves it was built to the team's quality bar

feedback.text: Correct — AC cover "does what was asked", the DoD covers "built well enough".

answer.text: Because acceptance criteria replace the need for any Definition of Done

feedback.text: AC do not replace the DoD; they answer different questions.

answer.text: Because the DoD lists the specific behaviours of that one story

feedback.text: The specific behaviours are the AC; the DoD is the generic quality bar.

answer.text: Because meeting either one alone always implies the other

feedback.text: They are independent: correct behaviour does not guarantee review, tests, or integration.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance criteria and the DoD answer different questions. AC: does the story do the specific thing asked of it? DoD: was it built to the shared quality standard (reviewed, tested, integrated, no critical defects)? A story can meet one without the other, so Done requires both.

name.text: Consequence of a weak Definition of Done

questiontext.text: What is the most likely consequence of a weak or unenforced Definition of Done?

answer.text: Untested, unreviewed work gets called "Done", so quality erodes and hidden work carries over later

feedback.text: Correct — a weak DoD lets incomplete work pass as done, deferring the real work.

answer.text: Stories become impossible to start

feedback.text: Starting is governed by the DoR; a weak DoD affects completion, not starting.

answer.text: Estimates automatically become more accurate

feedback.text: A weak DoD does not improve estimation; it hides remaining work.

answer.text: The team is forced to write more acceptance criteria

feedback.text: A weak DoD does not compel more AC; it lets low-quality work pass.

generalfeedback.text: When the DoD is weak or not enforced, work that is untested, unreviewed, or unintegrated gets marked Done. Quality erodes, "90% done" work hides remaining effort, and that effort resurfaces as carryover and defects later.

name.text: Consequence of a missing Definition of Ready

questiontext.text: What is the most likely consequence of having no effective Definition of Ready?

answer.text: Vague, unready items get pulled in and churn mid-sprint as the team discovers missing detail

feedback.text: Correct — without a DoR, unready work enters the sprint and thrashes.

answer.text: Completed work can never be marked Done

feedback.text: Marking work Done is governed by the DoD, not the DoR.

answer.text: The team is guaranteed to finish every story early

feedback.text: Unready work tends to slip, not finish early.

answer.text: Acceptance tests become unnecessary

feedback.text: A missing DoR does not remove the need for acceptance tests.

generalfeedback.text: Without a DoR, the team commits to items that are unclear, unestimated, or blocked by dependencies. Missing detail surfaces mid-sprint, forcing rework, blocked time, and churn — exactly what the entry gate exists to prevent.

name.text: What INVEST summarises

questiontext.text: The INVEST mnemonic (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) is most often used to check that a story is:

answer.text: Ready — it summarises qualities a good, ready-to-start story should have

feedback.text: Correct — INVEST is a readiness heuristic, closely tied to the DoR.

answer.text: Done — it lists the completion criteria for finished work

feedback.text: INVEST checks readiness of a story, not completeness of finished work.

answer.text: Released — it is a checklist for release notes

feedback.text: INVEST is about story quality for readiness, not release documentation.

answer.text: Over budget — it is a cost-tracking mnemonic

feedback.text: INVEST describes story qualities, not budget tracking.

generalfeedback.text: INVEST captures qualities of a well-formed story — Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. Estimable, Small, and Testable in particular map onto readiness, which is why INVEST is commonly used to support the Definition of Ready.

name.text: Classify small enough for one sprint

questiontext.text: "The story is small enough to finish within a single sprint." Which gate is this?

answer.text: A Definition of Ready item

feedback.text: Correct — being small enough to fit a sprint is a readiness condition.

answer.text: A Definition of Done item

feedback.text: Sizing is checked before starting, not at completion.

answer.text: An acceptance criterion describing the story's behaviour

feedback.text: Size is a readiness property, not a behavioural acceptance criterion.

answer.text: A release-level criterion

feedback.text: Fitting in a sprint gates entry, not release.

generalfeedback.text: Being small enough to complete in one sprint is a readiness property (the "S" in INVEST). If a story is too big it must be split before it is ready, so this belongs to the DoR.

name.text: Classify integrated with no critical defects

questiontext.text: "The change is integrated/merged and has no known critical defects." Which gate is this?

answer.text: A Definition of Done item

feedback.text: Correct — integration and freedom from critical defects are completion conditions.

answer.text: A Definition of Ready item

feedback.text: There is nothing to integrate before the work is built; this is completion.

answer.text: An estimate of the story's size

feedback.text: These are completeness conditions, not an estimate.

answer.text: A readiness condition, because defects are mentioned

feedback.text: Being defect-free after building is a completion concern, not readiness.

generalfeedback.text: Merging the work and confirming there are no known critical defects can only happen once the work exists, so both are DoD exit-gate criteria.

name.text: Meets AC but not DoD

questiontext.text: A story does everything its acceptance criteria require, but the code has not been reviewed and no tests were written. Is it Done?

answer.text: No — it fails the DoD, so it is not Done even though the AC are met

feedback.text: Correct — Done needs both the AC and the DoD; the DoD is unmet here.

answer.text: Yes — meeting the acceptance criteria is sufficient for Done

feedback.text: Meeting AC alone is not enough; the generic DoD must also hold.

answer.text: Yes — review and tests are optional extras

feedback.text: Review and tests are DoD criteria, not optional extras.

answer.text: It cannot be judged without re-estimating the story

feedback.text: Completeness is judged against AC and the DoD, not a re-estimate.

generalfeedback.text: The story behaves as required (AC met) but has not been reviewed or tested, so it fails the generic quality bar. Because Done requires both the AC and the DoD, the story is not Done.

name.text: Meets DoD but not its AC

questiontext.text: A change is reviewed, tested, and integrated, but it does not actually deliver the behaviour its acceptance criteria describe. Is the story Done?

answer.text: No — it satisfies the generic DoD but fails its own acceptance criteria

feedback.text: Correct — a well-built change that does the wrong thing still fails its AC.

answer.text: Yes — passing the DoD is enough to be Done

feedback.text: The DoD alone is not enough; the story must also meet its acceptance criteria.

answer.text: Yes — acceptance criteria are just suggestions

feedback.text: Acceptance criteria define what the story must do; they are not optional.

answer.text: Only the product owner's mood decides

feedback.text: Done is judged against the AC and the DoD, not mood.

generalfeedback.text: Here the work is high quality (DoD met) but solves the wrong problem (AC unmet). Done requires both, so a change that is well-built but does not meet its acceptance criteria is not Done.

name.text: Why the DoD is generic

questiontext.text: Why is the Definition of Done written as a generic checklist rather than per-story?

answer.text: So every story is held to the same consistent quality bar, whatever its specific behaviour

feedback.text: Correct — a generic DoD gives a uniform quality standard across all stories.

answer.text: So each story can define its own unique completion rules

feedback.text: Per-story rules are the acceptance criteria; the DoD is deliberately generic.

answer.text: Because the DoD only ever contains one item

feedback.text: The DoD usually has several items; being generic is about applying to all stories.

answer.text: Because generic checklists are easier to ignore

feedback.text: The point of a generic DoD is consistent enforcement, not ease of ignoring it.

generalfeedback.text: The DoD is generic precisely so it can act as a uniform quality bar: the same standard (reviewed, tested, integrated, no critical defects) applies to every story. Story-specific expectations live in the per-story acceptance criteria instead.

name.text: INVEST supports which gate

questiontext.text: A team uses INVEST when refining backlog items. Which gate does this most directly support?

answer.text: The Definition of Ready — INVEST helps confirm a story is well-formed and ready to start

feedback.text: Correct — INVEST is a readiness aid supporting the entry gate.

answer.text: The Definition of Done — INVEST lists completion checks

feedback.text: INVEST checks story readiness, not whether finished work is complete.

answer.text: Neither — INVEST is only about deployment

feedback.text: INVEST concerns story quality for readiness, not deployment.

answer.text: Both gates equally, since INVEST covers testing too

feedback.text: Although INVEST includes Testable, it assesses readiness of a story, so it supports the DoR.

generalfeedback.text: INVEST is applied during refinement to judge whether a story is well-formed and ready. Because that is exactly the concern of the entry gate, INVEST most directly supports the Definition of Ready.

name.text: Having AC versus meeting AC

questiontext.text: Which pairing correctly maps the two uses of acceptance criteria to their gates?

answer.text: Having clear, testable AC defined is a DoR item; the AC actually being met is part of the DoD

feedback.text: Correct — defining AC is readiness; satisfying them is part of completion.

answer.text: Having AC defined is a DoD item; meeting them is a DoR item

feedback.text: This is reversed: defining AC is readiness, meeting them is completion.

answer.text: Both defining and meeting AC belong only to the DoR

feedback.text: Meeting the AC can only happen once the work is built, so it is part of the DoD.

answer.text: Acceptance criteria play no role in either gate

feedback.text: AC feature in both: defined for readiness, met for completion.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance criteria touch both gates in different ways. For readiness (DoR), the story must have clear, testable AC defined. For completion (DoD), those AC must actually be satisfied by the built work. Confusing "defined" with "met" is a common source of gate errors.

name.text: DoR too loose causes churn

questiontext.text: A team pulls in stories that are only loosely understood. Mid-sprint they keep stopping to clarify scope and chase missing dependencies. Which gate is weak, and how does it show?

answer.text: The DoR is too loose, so unready work enters and churns mid-sprint

feedback.text: Correct — a loose entry gate lets unclear work in, causing mid-sprint thrash.

answer.text: The DoD is too strict, so nothing can be finished

feedback.text: The symptom is unready work entering, which points at the DoR, not a strict DoD.

answer.text: The acceptance criteria are too generic across stories

feedback.text: The problem is unready entry, a DoR weakness, not generic AC.

answer.text: Nothing is wrong; clarifying scope mid-sprint is ideal

feedback.text: Constant mid-sprint clarification is churn, a sign the DoR let unready work in.

generalfeedback.text: Stories that are unclear and dependency-blocked should not have passed the entry gate. When they do, the team discovers the gaps mid-sprint and churns. A loose DoR is the cause; tightening it prevents unready work from entering.

name.text: Which criterion is release-level DoD

questiontext.text: In a layered Definition of Done, which criterion most naturally belongs at the release level rather than per story?

answer.text: Full regression, performance, and security checks pass and release notes are prepared

feedback.text: Correct — cross-cutting regression, performance, security, and release notes are release-level.

answer.text: This story's code has been peer reviewed

feedback.text: Peer review of one story is a story-level DoD item.

answer.text: The unit tests for this story pass

feedback.text: Passing this story's unit tests is a story-level item.

answer.text: This story meets its own acceptance criteria

feedback.text: Meeting one story's AC is story-level, not release-level.

generalfeedback.text: A layered DoD has story, sprint/increment, and release levels. Cross-cutting concerns that only make sense for the whole product — full regression, performance and security testing, and release notes and sign-off — belong at the release level, not to each individual story.

name.text: Which criterion is story-level DoD

questiontext.text: In a layered Definition of Done, which criterion most naturally belongs at the story level?

answer.text: The story's code is reviewed, its unit tests pass, and it meets its acceptance criteria

feedback.text: Correct — review, unit tests, and meeting the AC are per-story completion items.

answer.text: The full product regression suite has been run

feedback.text: Whole-product regression is a release-level concern, not story-level.

answer.text: Formal performance and security sign-off for the release is obtained

feedback.text: Release sign-off is release-level, not story-level.

answer.text: Marketing release notes are approved

feedback.text: Release notes are a release-level item.

generalfeedback.text: Story-level DoD covers what one story needs to be complete: code reviewed, its unit and acceptance tests passing, and its acceptance criteria met with no known critical defects. Wider concerns escalate to the sprint/increment and release levels.

name.text: Why an untested story is not Done

questiontext.text: A developer says a feature "works on my machine — it's basically Done, just untested." Why is it not Done?

answer.text: Untested, unverified work has unknown quality, so calling it Done hides risk and remaining effort

feedback.text: Correct — without testing and review, quality is unknown and Done is a false claim.

answer.text: It is Done; running on the developer's machine satisfies the DoD

feedback.text: "Works on my machine" is not a DoD; it verifies nothing for others.

answer.text: It is Done as long as the code compiles

feedback.text: Compiling is not the DoD; testing, review, and integration are still required.

answer.text: It cannot be judged because the DoD does not cover testing

feedback.text: A proper DoD explicitly includes testing, which this work has not had.

generalfeedback.text: "Works on my machine" and "90% done" both disguise unverified work. Until it is tested, reviewed, and integrated, its real quality and the remaining effort are unknown. A DoD that includes testing exists precisely to stop such work being counted as Done.

name.text: DoR too strict becomes mini-waterfall

questiontext.text: A team makes its DoR so demanding that every story needs a full up-front design and complete specification before it may enter a sprint. What is the risk?

answer.text: It drifts toward a mini-waterfall and analysis-paralysis, front-loading heavy design before any coding

feedback.text: Correct — an over-strict DoR recreates big up-front analysis, the opposite of agile.

answer.text: Stories will always be too vague to start

feedback.text: That is the risk of a too-loose DoR, not a too-strict one.

answer.text: The DoD becomes impossible to satisfy

feedback.text: An over-strict DoR affects entry, not the completion criteria.

answer.text: Acceptance criteria become unnecessary

feedback.text: An over-strict DoR does not remove the need for acceptance criteria.

generalfeedback.text: A DoR should ensure enough clarity to start, not demand a complete design up front. Pushed too far it recreates a waterfall: heavy analysis and specification before any code, causing analysis-paralysis and delay. The balance is "ready enough to start", not "fully designed".

name.text: Balancing a too-loose DoR

questiontext.text: A too-loose DoR causes churn, while a too-strict DoR causes analysis-paralysis. What is the healthy balance?

answer.text: Require just enough clarity, sizing, and testable criteria to start confidently, refining details as work proceeds

feedback.text: Correct — "ready enough to start" avoids both churn and paralysis.

answer.text: Remove the DoR entirely so nothing blocks starting work

feedback.text: Removing it returns to churn from unready work.

answer.text: Require a complete, frozen specification for every story

feedback.text: That is the too-strict extreme causing analysis-paralysis.

answer.text: Let each developer decide readiness privately per story

feedback.text: The DoR is a shared team agreement, not a private per-person judgement.

generalfeedback.text: The DoR should guarantee a story is understood, sized, and has testable acceptance criteria and resolved dependencies — enough to start with confidence — while leaving room to refine detail during the sprint. Too loose causes mid-sprint churn; too strict recreates waterfall analysis.

name.text: Classify a specific behaviour versus generic bar

questiontext.text: "The API returns 404 for an unknown id" versus "all new code is covered by automated tests". How are these classified?

answer.text: The 404 behaviour is a per-story acceptance criterion; the test-coverage rule is a generic DoD item

feedback.text: Correct — the specific behaviour is AC; the blanket quality rule is DoD.

answer.text: The 404 behaviour is a DoD item; the test-coverage rule is an acceptance criterion

feedback.text: Reversed: specific behaviour is AC, the blanket rule is DoD.

answer.text: Both are acceptance criteria for that one story

feedback.text: The test-coverage rule applies to every story, so it is generic DoD, not AC.

answer.text: Both are generic DoD items

feedback.text: Returning 404 for an unknown id is specific to this story, so it is an AC.

generalfeedback.text: A statement about what this story specifically must do (return 404 for an unknown id) is an acceptance criterion. A blanket quality rule that applies to every story (all new code covered by tests) is a generic DoD item. Telling the specific from the generic is the key to classifying them.

name.text: Diagnose escaped defects from a bypassed DoD

questiontext.text: A team's velocity looks high, yet defects escaping to production keep rising and stories are marked Done without code review. Which gate is being violated?

answer.text: The Definition of Done — work is called complete without meeting its review and testing criteria

feedback.text: Correct — skipping review and testing while marking Done is a DoD violation.

answer.text: The Definition of Ready — the stories were unclear at the start

feedback.text: The symptom is completion without quality, which points at the DoD, not the DoR.

answer.text: The acceptance criteria — they were too specific

feedback.text: Escaped defects from skipped review point at the DoD, not overly specific AC.

answer.text: No gate — high velocity proves the process is healthy

feedback.text: High velocity with rising escaped defects signals the DoD is being bypassed.

generalfeedback.text: Marking work Done without review or tests inflates velocity while defects leak to production. That is a bypassed exit gate: the DoD is being violated. Enforcing the DoD realigns "Done" with genuine, verified completeness.

name.text: Diagnose a missing DoR

questiontext.text: Stories keep entering sprints with no estimate and no acceptance criteria, then balloon in scope and stall. Which gate is missing or violated?

answer.text: The Definition of Ready — unready items are being pulled into the sprint

feedback.text: Correct — unestimated, criteria-less items entering the sprint is a DoR failure.

answer.text: The Definition of Done — the finished work lacks quality

feedback.text: The problem is at entry (unready items), which is a DoR failure, not a DoD one.

answer.text: The release-level checklist — release notes are missing

feedback.text: The symptom is unready entry, not a release-documentation gap.

answer.text: None — ballooning scope is unavoidable

feedback.text: A DoR requiring estimation and clear AC would have caught these items at entry.

generalfeedback.text: Items lacking estimates and acceptance criteria should never have passed the entry gate. Because they did, scope is discovered mid-sprint and the work stalls. This is a missing or ignored DoR; enforcing readiness at entry prevents it.

name.text: What release-level DoD adds

questiontext.text: Beyond the story-level DoD, what does a release-level DoD typically add?

answer.text: Cross-cutting checks such as full regression, performance, security, release notes, and sign-off

feedback.text: Correct — release-level adds whole-product concerns beyond a single story.

answer.text: Nothing — it is identical to the story-level DoD

feedback.text: The release level adds whole-product concerns the story level cannot cover.

answer.text: Only the acceptance criteria of the last story in the release

feedback.text: Release-level DoD is about cross-cutting quality, not one story's AC.

answer.text: A relaxation of the story-level rules to speed up shipping

feedback.text: The release level adds stricter cross-cutting checks, it does not relax the story bar.

generalfeedback.text: Some quality concerns only make sense for the whole product at release: full regression across features, performance and security validation, documentation and release notes, and formal sign-off. A layered DoD places these at the release level, on top of the story-level and sprint/increment-level criteria.

name.text: Sprint-increment level DoD

questiontext.text: Which concern is best placed at the sprint/increment level of a layered DoD, between the story and release levels?

answer.text: The stories combine into an integrated, demoable increment deployed to a test environment

feedback.text: Correct — integrating stories into a shippable increment is an increment-level concern.

answer.text: This single story's unit tests pass

feedback.text: One story's unit tests are a story-level item.

answer.text: Formal external security sign-off for the public release

feedback.text: External release sign-off is a release-level concern.

answer.text: The wording of one story's acceptance criteria

feedback.text: A story's AC wording is a story-level detail, not an increment-level concern.

generalfeedback.text: Between story and release sits the increment level: individually-Done stories must integrate into a coherent, demoable increment, typically built and deployed to a test environment. Per-story checks stay at story level; whole-product gating stays at release level.

name.text: Why AC alone cannot declare Done

questiontext.text: Why are a story's acceptance criteria, on their own, not enough to declare it Done?

answer.text: They confirm the story does the right thing but not that it was built to the shared quality bar

feedback.text: Correct — AC cover correctness of behaviour, not review, testing, and integration.

answer.text: Because acceptance criteria are never testable

feedback.text: Good acceptance criteria are testable; the gap is that they do not cover the generic DoD.

answer.text: Because acceptance criteria are the same as the DoD

feedback.text: They are distinct: AC are per-story, the DoD is the generic quality bar.

answer.text: Because the DoD replaces the need for acceptance criteria

feedback.text: The DoD does not replace AC; both are needed for Done.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance criteria verify that the story delivers the specific behaviour asked of it, but they say nothing about whether it was reviewed, tested, integrated, and free of critical defects. Those generic quality concerns live in the DoD, so both are required for Done.

name.text: How DoD combats 90 percent done

questiontext.text: A team repeatedly hears "it's 90% done" for weeks. How does an explicit, enforced DoD combat this?

answer.text: It makes "Done" binary and objective, so hidden remaining work cannot be disguised as almost finished

feedback.text: Correct — a clear DoD turns fuzzy progress claims into a pass/fail check.

answer.text: It lets the team count 90%-done work as fully Done to keep morale up

feedback.text: Counting unfinished work as Done is exactly what a real DoD forbids.

answer.text: It speeds up coding so nothing is ever left at 90%

feedback.text: The DoD does not speed coding; it exposes the hidden remaining 10%.

answer.text: It removes the need to test the last 10%

feedback.text: The DoD requires that testing, so it does not remove it.

generalfeedback.text: The "90% done" problem hides an unknown, often large, remaining effort. An explicit DoD makes Done an objective, binary check: either every criterion is met or the story is not Done. That surfaces the hidden work instead of letting it hide behind a comfortable percentage.

name.text: Layer for performance under load

questiontext.text: "The system meets its performance-under-load SLA." In a layered DoD, where does this criterion most naturally sit?

answer.text: At the release (or increment) level, as a cross-cutting whole-system concern — not on every individual story

feedback.text: Correct — system-wide performance is validated at the release/increment level.

answer.text: On every single story, as a per-story acceptance criterion

feedback.text: Whole-system load performance is not meaningfully checked per tiny story; it is cross-cutting.

answer.text: In the DoR, as a readiness condition

feedback.text: Performance is verified after building, not as an entry condition.

answer.text: Nowhere — performance is not part of any DoD

feedback.text: System performance is a legitimate release-level DoD concern.

generalfeedback.text: Performance under load is a property of the integrated system, not of one small story, so it is validated at the release or increment level of a layered DoD. Attaching it to every story would be both impractical and misleading.

name.text: Diagnose skipped-testing carryover

questiontext.text: Each sprint the team marks code-complete stories Done and defers their testing "to next sprint". Carryover grows and surprises appear late. What is the diagnosis and fix?

answer.text: The DoD (which must include testing) is being violated; enforce it so stories are only Done when tested, exposing the real remaining work

feedback.text: Correct — deferring testing while marking Done violates the DoD and hides work.

answer.text: The DoR is too strict; loosen it so more stories can start

feedback.text: The failure is at completion (testing deferred), so it is a DoD problem, not a strict DoR.

answer.text: Nothing is wrong; deferring testing a sprint is standard practice

feedback.text: Deferring testing while calling work Done is an anti-pattern that hides carryover.

answer.text: The acceptance criteria are too generic and should be removed

feedback.text: The problem is skipped testing at the exit gate, not the AC wording.

generalfeedback.text: Marking work Done while deferring its testing violates a DoD that includes testing. It inflates completed counts, builds hidden test debt, and forces carryover and late surprises. The fix is to enforce the DoD so a story is Done only when it is actually tested, making the real remaining work visible now.

name.text: Stories Done but increment not shippable

questiontext.text: Every story passed its story-level DoD, yet when combined the increment fails a full regression run and cannot be released. What does this reveal about the team's DoD?

answer.text: The layered DoD is incomplete: story-level checks passed, but increment/release-level integration and regression criteria are missing or unenforced

feedback.text: Correct — passing story-level does not guarantee the integrated increment; higher layers are needed.

answer.text: Nothing — if every story is Done, the release is automatically Done too

feedback.text: Individually-Done stories can still break each other; that is why higher DoD layers exist.

answer.text: The DoR was too loose, so the stories should not have started

feedback.text: The stories were ready and individually complete; the gap is at the integration/release layer.

answer.text: The acceptance criteria were too specific to each story

feedback.text: Specific per-story AC are fine; the missing piece is cross-cutting integration and regression.

generalfeedback.text: Stories that are each Done can still interact badly once integrated. A layered DoD anticipates this: the increment/release levels add integration, full regression, and cross-cutting checks. If those layers are missing or unenforced, an increment of individually-Done stories can still be un-shippable — exactly the gap seen here.
